Where it began

Mohammad Junaid Khan was born on 24 December 1989 in Swabi, a place that had never before produced a cricketer of note. He was not much interested in the game at first. He played with a taped tennis ball until a cousin got him started with the hard one, and at 16 he was timed as the quickest bowler in a provincial Twenty20 competition.

Teammates nudged him towards the Under-17 trials in Abbottabad. He nearly stayed away, but went, and Ehteshamuddin saw enough to send him to Lahore. He made his first-class debut for Abbottabad in January 2007, aged 17, taking 4 for 57, and spent four seasons as their spearhead.

The player

He first joined the Pakistan squad as a late call-up for the 2011 World Cup, without an international match to his name, and made his one-day debut in the West Indies that April. A few weeks later he was man of the match in Ireland with four wickets for twelve runs.

His Test debut came against Zimbabwe on 1 September 2011, and the next month, against Sri Lanka, he took his first five-wicket haul on a pitch made for batting. Pakistan won that series 1–0 and he took 12 wickets in it. Sri Lanka stayed his favourite opponents: his best innings figures of 5 for 38 came against them, and so did his 50th Test wicket, in only his 14th Test.

He played 22 Tests from 2011 to 2015 and took 71 wickets at 31.73, with five five-wicket innings. He was part of the Pakistan side that won the 2017 Champions Trophy and was picked in the team of the tournament.

What made him special

He built his action on Wasim Akram's and also studied clips of Imran Khan. He called himself a line-and-length man, trusting accuracy to bring the wickets, and he could move the ball both ways at around 140 km/h. A spell at Lancashire, on Akram's recommendation, taught him the yorker and how to use English conditions. In Port Elizabeth in 2013 he defended nine runs in the last over to win a one-day game by a single run.

His batting was more cheerful than fruitful. His top Test score was 17, though he was not out in 11 of his 28 innings, which shows a certain stubbornness.

Away from the middle

His cousin Yasir Shah, the leg-spinner, followed him into the Pakistan side. After playing he moved into coaching. In August 2023 he became head coach of the Islamabad region and helped them win promotion to first-class cricket. He was Pakistan's Under-19 bowling coach at the 2024 Under-19 World Cup, and in June 2024 he became bowling coach of the Pakistan women's team.

And finally

He began his run-up with a big skip and a jump, the kind of flourish that tells a batsman something is coming. For a boy who could barely be bothered with cricket, that is quite a lot of enthusiasm.
